sense: not under another’s rule or control

terms.grammar: phrase: the genitive of jūs, “of one’s own right”, usually with esse
terms.comment: In law, a person in no one else’s power, neither a father’s nor a master’s; Cicero uses it of jurors too independent to be managed. Morgan–Owens gives it for an independent state, and suī jūris fierī for gaining independence (after Egger).

evidence: Caes. BG 1.45.3: līberam dēbēre esse Galliam
terms.comment: The plain word for a free people (see free). Independence itself is lībertās (M-O s.v. independence).

terms.gloss: be self-governing: live under one’s own laws
evidence: M-O s.v. independence: facultās suīs lēgibus ūtendī (Egger)
terms.comment: What Rome left to a free city or people it did not rule directly.

phrases.latin: līberam dēbēre esse Galliam, quam bellō victam suīs lēgibus ūtī voluisset
phrases.english: Gaul ought to be free, since the senate, though it had beaten her in war, had chosen to let her live under her own laws

phrases.latin: quod eōs in jūdicandō nimium suī jūris sententiaeque cognōsset
phrases.english: because he knew them to be too independent, too much of their own mind, when they sat in judgment

sources: Lewis & Short: jus · Lewis & Short: liber · Lewis & Short: utor
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. independent; independence.
Caesar, Gallic War 1.45, and Cicero, Verrines 2.1.18, checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
